title: Level 2 – International Qualified Nurse
subtitle: Child Health Nursing
intro: Caring for Children and Families Welcome to GNPS Level 2 - International Qualified Nurse. International paediatric practice expects nurses to integrate developmental assessment, evidence-based care, family partnership, safeguarding responsibilities and structured escalation. This level bridges national nursing preparation with international expectations. It strengthens your ability to manage complex childhood conditions, interpret paediatric trends, calculate medicines safely, communicate across cultures and coordinate multidisciplinary care. Throughout this level you will strengthen your ability to: Apply internationally recognised paediatric assessment frameworks Prioritise care using age-specific physiological risk Recognise and escalate paediatric deterioration Manage common high-risk childhood conditions Apply paediatric medication and infusion safety principles Support children with chronic illness and developmental needs Provide trauma-informed and culturally safe care Recognise safeguarding concerns and follow reporting pathways Coordinate discharge, education and continuity of care International practice requires nurses to interpret symptoms within age, development, family context and clinical trends. A normal adult value may be abnormal for a child, and a quiet child may be more concerning than a distressed one. By completing Level 2, you should be able to deliver safe, culturally responsive and evidence-informed paediatric care while meeting the professional expectations of international healthcare environments.

content.text: International paediatric practice expects nurses to combine structured assessment with developmental knowledge and clinical judgement. Children can compensate until late in illness, so subtle trends and caregiver concerns must be taken seriously.
Learning outcomes
Apply structured paediatric assessment frameworks Prioritise care using age-specific risk
Interpret trends and caregiver observations Escalate deterioration using structured communication
Structured Assessment ABCDE supports urgent assessment, while tools such as the paediatric assessment triangle help evaluate appearance, breathing and circulation quickly.

Age-Specific Interpretation Vital signs and expected behaviours vary by age. Tachycardia, tachypnoea, delayed capillary refill or altered interaction should be interpreted within developmental context.
Family Observations Parents may notice subtle behavioural change before measurements become abnormal. Statements such as 'this is not my child' should prompt assessment.
Escalation Structured communication should identify the child, age, weight, current concern, relevant history, assessment findings and action required.

A parent says her child is unusually sleepy after minor surgery. Vital signs are near the expected range, but the child is difficult to rouse and breathing more slowly. The nurse recognises possible opioid-related deterioration and escalates immediately.
Key learning points
Combine assessment tools with clinical judgement Interpret all findings within age and development
Listen carefully to parents and carers Escalate based on concern, not only scoring thresholds
High-risk paediatric conditions can deteriorate rapidly. Nurses must anticipate complications, deliver age-appropriate interventions and coordinate care with specialist teams.
Learning outcomes
Manage common high-risk paediatric conditions Recognise airway, neurological and circulatory emergencies
Apply safe emergency interventions Evaluate response to treatment
Respiratory Emergencies Severe asthma, upper-airway obstruction and respiratory failure require rapid assessment, oxygenation support, medication and preparation for escalation.
Neurological Emergencies Prolonged seizure, meningitis and increased intracranial pressure require airway protection, neurological monitoring and urgent treatment.
Circulatory and Infectious Emergencies Sepsis, shock and severe dehydration may present with tachycardia, poor perfusion, altered behaviour and reduced urine output. Hypotension can be a late sign.
Metabolic Emergencies Diabetic ketoacidosis and severe electrolyte abnormalities require careful fluid, insulin and neurological monitoring according to paediatric protocols.

A child with fever develops a non-blanching rash, prolonged capillary refill and lethargy. The nurse recognises possible sepsis, activates the emergency pathway, obtains appropriate access and supports urgent treatment without waiting for hypotension.
Key learning points
Hypotension may occur late in paediatric shock Treat airway and breathing changes urgently
Use paediatric-specific emergency protocols Monitor response continuously

sections.title: Complex Medication, Chronic Illness and Discharge Care

content.text: Children with chronic or complex conditions may rely on multiple medicines, devices and caregivers. Safe care requires precise calculation, education and coordination across hospital, school and community settings.
Learning outcomes
Apply advanced paediatric medication safety Support children with chronic and complex conditions
Coordinate care across services Prepare families for safe discharge

Medication and Infusion Safety Weight-based dosing, concentration, infusion rate, compatibility and maximum dose must be checked. Smart pumps and electronic systems support but do not replace verification.
Chronic Conditions Asthma, diabetes, epilepsy, cystic fibrosis, congenital heart disease and disability require long-term plans that support development, education and family life.
Transition and Coordination Care plans may involve paediatricians, nurses, pharmacists, therapists, school staff, primary care and community services. Responsibilities should be clear.
Family Education Families need practical instruction about medicines, equipment, warning signs, emergency plans and follow-up. Teach-back and return demonstration confirm understanding.

A child with epilepsy is discharged with rescue medication. The nurse teaches both parents, provides a written seizure plan, checks the dose against current weight and asks each caregiver to demonstrate administration before discharge.
Key learning points
Recalculate doses when the child's weight changes Coordinate care across home, school and health services
Use teach-back and return demonstration Provide clear emergency action plans

sections.title: Safeguarding, Communication and Culturally Safe Care

content.text: International paediatric nurses must uphold children's rights, recognise safeguarding concerns and communicate in ways that respect culture, family structure and the child's developing autonomy.
Learning outcomes
Recognise safeguarding risks Communicate with children and families across cultures
Support assent, consent and privacy Apply trauma-informed principles
Safeguarding Responsibilities Nurses should recognise physical, emotional and behavioural indicators of abuse or neglect and follow local legal and organisational pathways promptly.
Communication Access Professional interpreters should be used for complex information. Children should receive explanations suited to age and ability.

Consent and Assent Parents or guardians usually provide legal consent, while children should be involved in decisions according to maturity. Adolescents require privacy within legal and safety limits.
Trauma-Informed Care Predictability, choice, calm communication and minimising unnecessary restraint can reduce distress for children who have experienced trauma.

An adolescent asks to speak privately about medication and home safety. The nurse explains confidentiality and its limits, listens without judgement and follows the safeguarding pathway when immediate risk is disclosed.
Key learning points
Know local safeguarding and consent requirements Explain confidentiality honestly
Use professional interpreters when needed Support children's participation in decisions

End-of-Program Summary By completing GNPS Program 7 - Level 2, you have strengthened your ability to assess deteriorating children, manage high-risk conditions, apply complex medication safety, coordinate chronic care and uphold safeguarding responsibilities. You are now prepared for Level 3, where the focus moves to leadership, system improvement and global child health.
